Suppose first that a simple continued fraction is eventually periodic. Its periodic tail ξ is fixed by the Möbius transformation represented by the continued-fraction matrix of one full period:
ξ=cξ+daξ+b​.
(1)
Thus
cξ2+(d−a)ξ−b=0.
(2)
The infinite tail is not rational, since a rational simple continued fraction terminates. Hence ξ is a quadratic irrational, and the finite initial block expresses the original number as another rational Möbius transform of ξ. Therefore every eventually periodic simple continued fraction represents a quadratic irrational.
For the purely periodic fraction x=[7,7,7,…],
x=7+x1​,
(3)
so x2−7x−1=0. Positivity selects
x=27+53​​.​
(4)
Apply the continued-fraction algorithm to 23​:
23​=4+123​−4​1​=4+1+3+1+8+⋯1​1​1​1​.
(5)
The complete quotient then repeats, giving
23​=[4;1,3,1,8​].​
(6)
The convergents through one term before the final 8 are
4,5,419​,524​.
(7)
The last of these satisfies the Pell equation
242−23⋅52=576−575=1,
(8)
so a positive solution is
(x,y)=(24,5).​
(9)

Solution

Words: 168
3H OurBigBook.com
A binary linear-feedback shift register of length L stores L bits. At each clock it outputs one bit, shifts the state, and inserts a fixed linear combination over F2​ of the stored bits. Equivalently, its output obeys a recurrence
sn​=c1​sn−1​+⋯+cL​sn−L​.
(17)
The Berlekamp-Massey algorithm processes the observed symbols from left to right. It maintains the shortest current connection polynomial C(D), its degree L, and a saved polynomial from the most recent degree increase. At step n it computes the discrepancy
dn​=sn​+∑i=1L​ci​sn−i​.
(18)
If dn​=0, the current recurrence already predicts the new symbol. If dn​=0, a shifted multiple of the saved polynomial is added to C to cancel the discrepancy; when 2L≤n, the algorithm also replaces L by n+1−L and saves the old polynomial.
For the observed binary sequence, the nonzero-discrepancy updates are
n146​L234​C(D)1+D21+D2+D31+D3+D4.​​
(19)
All discrepancies through n=11 then vanish. Thus the shortest recurrence is
sn​=sn−3​+sn−4​(mod2),​
(20)
or, equivalently, sn+4​=sn+1​+sn​. The connection polynomial is 1+D3+D4, and with the reciprocal convention the feedback polynomial is
x4+x+1.​
(21)

Fix an effective enumeration fe,n​ of the n-ary partial recursive functions.
The S-m-n theorem says that program inputs can be compiled into an index: for every m,n≥1 there is a total recursive snm​ such that
fsnm​(e,x1​,…,xm​),n​(y1​,…,yn​)≃fe,m+n​(x1​,…,xm​,y1​,…,yn​).
(22)
Here ≃ means that either both sides are undefined or both are defined and equal.
The recursion theorem says that every total recursive transformation h of program indices has a semantic fixed point: some e satisfies
fe,1​≃fh(e),1​.
(23)
The Rice theorem says that every nontrivial extensional property of programs computed by partial recursive functions is undecidable.

5J (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 169 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 169
5J OurBigBook.com
With Control as the reference group, the fitted normal linear model has mean
E[Weight]=β0​+βTime​t+βTreat​ITreat​+βInt​tITreat​+cage effect.
(33)
Thus the control-group rate is βTime​, while the treatment-group rate is βTime​+βInt​. The estimates are
control slope​=−0.006023,​
(34)
and
treatment slope​=−0.006023−0.173515=−0.179538​
(35)
weight units per day. The control slope has t=−0.477 and p=0.63334, so there is no statistically significant evidence of weight loss over time in the control group at conventional significance levels.
The plotted regression residuals for each mouse form smooth time patterns rather than an unstructured cloud: nearby observations on the same mouse have similar residuals, and the mice also show persistent individual offsets. This is strong evidence of autocorrelation and omitted mouse-level variation. The ordinary linear model treats all 400 measurements as independent after accounting for cage, so it commits pseudoreplication and will generally underestimate the coefficient standard errors. The reported t-tests and p-values should therefore not be trusted. A random-intercept linear mixed model with a within-mouse correlation structure would respect the repeated-measures design.

Let a one-parameter infinitesimal transformation be δqi​=ϵXi​(q,t) and suppose its change in the Lagrangian is a total derivative,
δL=ϵdtdF​.
(50)
With canonical momentum pi​=∂L/∂q˙​i​, the chain rule and the Euler-Lagrange equations give, along a motion,
δL=ϵ∑i​(∂qi​∂L​Xi​+pi​dtdXi​​)=ϵdtd​∑i​pi​Xi​.
(51)
Comparison with the assumed total derivative proves Noether theorem:
J=i∑​pi​Xi​−Fis conserved.​
(52)
The given Lagrangian has no explicit time dependence, so its energy function is conserved:
E=x˙∂x˙∂L​+y˙​∂y˙​∂L​−L=2y2x˙2+y˙​2​+V(yx​).​
(53)
It is also invariant under the dilation (x,y)↦(eϵx,eϵy): the velocities and y all scale by the same factor, while x/y is unchanged. The generator is (Xx​,Xy​)=(x,y) and F=0. Since
px​=y2x˙​,py​=y2y˙​​,
(54)
Noether's theorem supplies the second first integral
D=xpx​+ypy​=y2xx˙+yy˙​​.​
(55)
The integrals E and D are independent on an open dense subset of phase space.

c OurBigBook.com
No classical one-query algorithm can determine x0​ with certainty. If it queries a string x and receives 1, then it knows x0​=x. But if it receives 0, each of the other three strings remains compatible with the response. Randomization cannot remove this ambiguity when certainty is required. Thus
one classical query is insufficient.​
(69)
Indeed, three adaptive classical queries are necessary and sufficient in the worst case: after three negative answers, the unqueried fourth string must be x0​.

The Fermat-Euler theorem states that
gcd(a,n)=1⟹aφ(n)≡1(modn).
(70)
Indeed, if r1​,…,rφ(n)​ are the reduced residue classes modulo n, multiplication by a permutes them. Therefore
∏i​ari​≡∏i​ri​(modn).
(71)
The product ∏i​ri​ is invertible modulo n, so cancellation gives the theorem.
Now let p be prime. If k≡1(modp−1), then for p∤b, Fermat little theorem gives bk−1≡1(modp), while p∣b makes bk≡b≡0. Thus bk≡b for every integer b.
Conversely, assume this congruence holds for every b. Choose a primitive root g modulo p. Then gk−1≡1(modp). Since g has order p−1, one has p−1∣k−1. Hence
bk≡b(modp) for every b⟺k≡1(modp−1).​

b OurBigBook.com
An odd composite N coprime to b is a Fermat pseudoprime to base b when bN−1≡1(modN). It is a Carmichael number when this congruence holds for every b coprime to N.
Suppose a Carmichael number has pa∥N with a≥2. The group (Z/paZ)∗ is cyclic, so choose a residue of order
φ(pa)=pa−1(p−1).
(73)
By the Chinese remainder theorem, extend it to an integer b that is congruent to 1 modulo every other prime-power factor of N. Then gcd(b,N)=1, and the Carmichael congruence forces the order of b modulo pa to divide N−1. In particular p∣N−1, contradicting p∣N. Therefore every Carmichael number is square-free.
Now assume N is square-free. If p−1∣N−1 for every p∣N, then for every b coprime to N, Fermat little theorem gives
bN−1≡1(modp)
(74)
for each p∣N. The Chinese remainder theorem then gives the congruence modulo N, so N is Carmichael.
Conversely, if N is Carmichael, fix p∣N. Choose a primitive root g modulo p and use the Chinese remainder theorem to choose b≡g(modp) and b≡1(modN/p). Then bN−1≡1(modp), so the order p−1 of g divides N−1. This proves the Korselt criterion in the required form:
N is Carmichael⟺N is square-free and p−1∣N−1 for every p∣N.​
(75)
A Carmichael number cannot have one prime factor because it is composite. If N=pq with distinct primes p<q, the condition q−1∣pq−1 implies q−1∣p−1, which is impossible. Hence every Carmichael number has at least three prime factors.

The divisibility conditions include
q−1∣pr−1,p−1∣qr−1.
(76)
Write
pr−1=b(q−1)
(77)
for a positive integer b. Since p<q,
pr−1<r(q−1),
(78)
so 1≤b<r. Moreover,
q=bpr+b−1​.

Multiplying the second divisibility by b and reducing modulo p−1 gives
p−1∣b(qr−1)=pr2+r(b−1)−b≡(r−1)(r+b)(modp−1).
(80)
The positive integer on the right is at most (r−1)(2r−1). Consequently
p≤(r−1)(2r−1)+1.
(81)
There are only finitely many possible primes p and integers b∈{1,…,r−1}, and each pair determines at most one q=(pr+b−1)/b. Therefore
for fixed r, only finitely many prime pairs (p,q) make pqr Carmichael.​

The epsilon-recursion theorem says that for every definable operation G assigning a set G(x,h) to each set x and each function h with domain x, there is a unique class function F such that
F(x)=G(x,F↾x)​
(117)
for every set x.
For uniqueness, suppose F and F′ both satisfy the recursion. If they agree on every y∈x, then their restrictions to x agree and hence
F(x)=G(x,F↾x)=G(x,F′↾x)=F′(x).
(118)
The epsilon induction principle therefore gives F=F′.
For existence, call a function f coherent on a transitive set T when
f(z)=G(z,f↾z)(z∈T).
(119)
The same epsilon-induction argument shows that any two coherent functions agree on the intersection of their transitive domains. Assuming coherent functions have been constructed below every member of x, their compatible union defines all values below x; adjoining the value prescribed by G(x,⋅) extends the construction to x. Epsilon induction establishes this construction for every x. The compatible local functions therefore unite to the required class function F.
A relation r on x is well-founded when every nonempty subset of x has an element with no r-predecessor in that subset. It is extensional when
{b:bra}={b:bra′}⟹a=a′.
(120)
The Mostowski collapse theorem states that every well-founded extensional relation (x,r) is isomorphic to membership on a unique transitive set M. Define recursively
π(a)={π(b):bra}.
(121)
Well-founded recursion makes π well defined. Epsilon-style induction along r, together with extensionality, shows that π is injective. By definition,
bra⟺π(b)∈π(a),
(122)
so π is an isomorphism from (x,r) onto (M,∈), where M=ranπ. If z∈π(a)∈M, then z=π(b) for some bra, so z∈M; hence M is transitive. If another collapse π′ has transitive range, induction gives π′(a)={π′(b):bra}=π(a), proving uniqueness.
Finally, suppose x is finite. Its collapse M is a finite transitive set, so every member of M is hereditarily finite. Therefore every well-founded extensional relation on x collapses to a transitive subset of Vω​.
Conversely, let x be infinite. Choose the initial infinite ordinal κ equinumerous with x. The successor ordinal κ+1 has the same cardinality as κ. Pulling its membership relation back along a bijection x→κ+1 gives a well-founded extensional relation on x whose collapse is κ+1. But κ∈κ+1 is not hereditarily finite, so κ+1⊈Vω​. Consequently,
the required sets x are exactly the finite sets.​
(123)

Let H denote a hyperplane-section divisor of a projective plane curve. The adjunction formula for a smooth degree-d projective plane curve states
KC​∼(d−3)H∣C​.
(206)
Since deg(H∣C​)=d, this gives the canonical degree of a smooth plane curve
degKC​=d(d−3)​.
(207)
Combining this with degKC​=2g−2 gives the genus of a smooth plane curve
g(C)=2(d−1)(d−2)​​.
(208)
Homogenization of the affine equation gives the projective completion
C=V(F)⊂P2,F(X,Y,Z)=X3Z+XY3+YZ3.
(209)
This is the plane model y plus x cubed plus xy cubed equals zero of the Klein quartic: after the coordinate relabelling [A:B:C]=[Y:X:Z], its equation is A3B+B3C+C3A=0.
Its first partial derivatives are
FX​=3X2Z+Y3,FY​=3XY2+Z3,FZ​=X3+3YZ2.
(210)
If one of X,Y,Z vanishes at a common zero of these three derivatives, the displayed equations successively force all three coordinates to vanish, which is impossible in projective space. If XYZ=0, multiplying the three derivative equations gives
X3Y3Z3=−27X3Y3Z3,
(211)
again a contradiction. The Jacobian criterion therefore proves that C is smooth.
The rational function y=Y/Z defines a rational map of projective varieties C⇢P1. Because C is a smooth projective curve, it extends uniquely to a morphism
π:C⟶P1.
(212)
For a generic finite value of y, its fibre is given by the cubic
x3+y3x+y=0,
(213)
so the degree of a holomorphic map is 3. The discriminant of a depressed cubic is
Δ(y)=−4y9−27y2=−y2(4y7+27).
(214)
At y=0 the fibre consists of (0,0). Since Fy​(0,0)=1, the holomorphic implicit function theorem gives
y=−x3+O(x10),
(215)
so x is a local coordinate and π has ramification index of a holomorphic map 3 there. Each of the seven distinct roots of 4y7+27 gives one double, but not triple, root of the cubic in x, hence seven further ramification points of index 2.
It remains to inspect the points at infinity. They are
P=[1:0:0],Q=[0:1:0].
(216)
Near Q, set u=X/Y and v=Z/Y. The equation becomes u3v+u+v3=0, so u=−v3+O(v10), while y=1/v has a simple pole. Thus eQ​=1. Near P, set s=Y/X and t=Z/X. Now t+s3+st3=0, so t=−s3+O(s10) and
y=ts​=−s−2(1+O(s7)).
(217)
Thus y has a double pole at P and eP​=2. These calculations are the ramification of the x-coordinate on the Klein quartic after the coordinate relabelling above.
The total ramification contribution is
(3−1)+7(2−1)+(2−1)=10.
(218)
The Riemann-Hurwitz formula for the degree-three map to the projective line now gives
2g(C)−2=3(−2)+10=4,
(219)
and therefore
g(C)=3​.

Suppose that a connected smooth surface S⊂R3 properly contains S. Since S and S have the same dimension, S is open in S. Choose a point of its relative boundary. Inside a sufficiently small compact normal neighbourhood in S, choose q∈S and a closest point p∈S∖S. A minimizing S-geodesic from q to p stays in S before its endpoint, since encountering the complement earlier would contradict the choice of p.
The restriction of this curve is consequently a geodesic of S with a finite maximal endpoint at p. On the other hand, the Gaussian curvature of S is the restriction of the smooth Gaussian curvature of S, so it remains bounded near p. This contradicts condition (∗). Hence
S=S​,

so S is an inextendible embedded surface. This is the curvature-blowup criterion for inextendibility of a surface.

32E (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 291 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 291
32E OurBigBook.com
An interval map has a horseshoe for an interval map when two disjoint subintervals are each mapped across a common interval. It is Glendinning-chaotic when one of its positive iterates has such a horseshoe.
Let the points of the three-cycle be x1​<x2​<x3​ and put I0​=[x1​,x2​], I1​=[x2​,x3​]. There are two possible cyclic orders. If x1​↦x2​↦x3​↦x1​, the intermediate value theorem gives
I0​⟶I1​,I1​⟶I0​,I1​⟶I1​
(288)
for the interval covering relation. Thus there are two closed covering walks of length two based at I1​. In the reverse cyclic order there are instead the arrows I0​→I0​, I0​→I1​ and I1​→I0​, again giving two closed walks of length two. The horseshoe from two closed covering walks therefore shows that F2 has a horseshoe in either case, so F is chaotic.
The Sharkovsky theorem orders the positive integers as
3≺5≺7≺⋯≺2⋅3≺2⋅5≺⋯≺22⋅3≺⋯≺⋯≺23≺22≺2≺1,
(289)
and says that a cycle of a given period forces cycles of every period to its right.
Suppose N=2rq with q>1 odd. Then F2r has a q-cycle. The Sharkovsky theorem gives that map a six-cycle, and squaring it produces a three-cycle. Hence F2r+1 has a three-cycle and an iterate of F has a horseshoe. Thus
N not a power of two and an N-cycle⟹F is Glendinning-chaotic.​
(290)
A horseshoe contains the symbolic dynamics of the Bernoulli shift. Periodic binary words give cycles of every symbolic period; after translating from an iterate back to F, this supplies cycles of many periods that are not powers of two.
For the logistic map, a ten-cycle would imply chaos because 10 is not a power of two. Hence there is no ten-cycle for μ<μ∞​. A three-cycle forces every period, so a ten-cycle exists for μ>1+8​. The stated facts alone give no conclusion for the intermediate range:
μ<μ∞​: extnoten−cycle;μ>1+8​: extaten−cycleexists.​
(291)

A three-dimensional Bravais lattice is the set of all integer combinations of three linearly independent primitive vectors. Its reciprocal lattice is
Λ∗={G:G⋅R∈2πZ for every R∈Λ},
(300)
and the first Brillouin zone is the Wigner-Seitz cell of the origin in reciprocal space.
For the stated FCC lattice, the primitive-cell volume is
Ω=a1​⋅(a2​×a3​)=4a3​.
(301)
The reciprocal-basis formula gives
b1​=a2π​(−e1​+e2​+e3​),b2​=a2π​(e1​−e2​+e3​),b3​=a2π​(e1​+e2​−e3​)​.
(302)
A reciprocal primitive cell, and hence the Brillouin zone, has volume
Ω(2π)3​=a332π3​​.
(303)
In the first Born approximation, with momentum transfer q=k−k′, the scattering amplitude is
fV​(k;k′)=−2πℏ2m​∫R3​eiq⋅rV(r)d3r.
(304)
For the spherical shell, align the polar axis with q and use its radial Dirac delta function:
∫eiq⋅rV0​δ(r−d)d3r=4πV0​d2qdsin(qd)​.
(305)
Therefore
f​V​(k;k′)=−ℏ22mV0​d2​qdsin(qd)​​.
(306)
Translation of each atomic potential multiplies its transform by a phase, so the crystal lattice structure factor gives
fVΛ​​(k;k′)=f​V​(k;k′)∑R∈Λ​eiq⋅R.
(307)
For an infinite lattice, the lattice Poisson summation formula turns the sum into
∑R∈Λ​eiq⋅R=Ω(2π)3​∑G∈Λ∗​δ(3)(q−G).
(308)
Thus the amplitude vanishes away from reciprocal-lattice momentum transfers.
In elastic scattering, ∣k∣=∣k′∣ and hence
∣q∣=2ksin2θ​.
(309)
The two shortest relevant reciprocal-vector lengths of this FCC lattice are
∣G2​∣=a2π3​​,∣G1​∣=a4π​.
(310)
Both are kinematically available when k>2π/a. Assigning their scattering angles θ2​ and θ1​, respectively, gives
sin(θ2​/2)sin(θ1​/2)​=∣G2​∣∣G1​∣​=3​2​​.
(311)
